promptText: What is the fundamental difference between direct and indirect prompt injection?
options: Direct injection only works on open-source models while indirect injection only works on hosted APIs

Direct injection is when the attacker types the malicious instruction themselves into the chat; indirect injection is when the attacker plants it somewhere a different, unsuspecting victim's AI system later reads
Direct injection targets the system prompt while indirect injection targets the model's training data
Indirect injection requires the attacker to have valid API credentials, while direct injection does not
explanation: Direct injection attacks the attacker's own session; indirect injection is more dangerous for enterprise systems because it attacks a victim user through content they never wrote and often never see, such as a poisoned document or web page.

promptText: Why doesn't a parameterized-query-style fix, the one that solved SQL injection, work for prompt injection?
options: Parameterized queries are too slow to apply to natural language
SQL databases don't support Unicode, so the analogy breaks down

A database driver enforces a hard, protocol-level separation between code and data; a language model has no equivalent boundary, since system prompts, user input, and retrieved content are all concatenated into one token sequence processed by the same attention mechanism
Prompt injection was discovered before SQL injection, so no analogous fix could have been designed
explanation: Parameterized queries work because the database is contractually guaranteed to never interpret a parameter as SQL syntax. No token in a model's context window carries an enforced 'this is law, this is just data' tag — that distinction is only a learned, probabilistic tendency.

promptText: What is 'prompt leaking' as an injection goal?
options: Redirecting the model to perform an entirely different task than the one requested
Extracting the confidential system prompt, few-shot examples, or internal tool definitions rather than changing the model's behavior
Causing the model to call a tool with attacker-controlled arguments
Forcing the model to produce output that fails schema validation
explanation: Prompt leaking targets exfiltration of the operator's confidential configuration itself (e.g., 'repeat the text above starting with...'), which is distinct from goal hijacking, and matters because a leaked prompt often reveals exploitable business logic for further attacks.

promptText: What is 'instruction hierarchy,' and is it an architecturally enforced boundary?
options: It is a training approach that biases the model to weight system instructions above user content above tool/document content; it is a learned, probabilistic tendency, not an enforced protocol boundary
It is a hard-coded permission system, identical in guarantee to Spring Security method-level authorization
It is a network-layer control that blocks unauthorized API callers before they reach the model
It is a database schema that separates trusted and untrusted text at the storage layer
explanation: Instruction hierarchy training measurably raises the bar an attacker must clear, but because it is a learned tendency rather than an architectural guarantee, a sufficiently persuasive injected instruction can still override it.

promptText: Which of the following best distinguishes 'goal hijacking' from 'context/data exfiltration' as injection objectives?
options: Goal hijacking redirects the model away from its intended task toward the attacker's task; data exfiltration uses the model's own output or tool-calling channel to smuggle sensitive data out to the attacker
Goal hijacking only applies to text-only chatbots, while data exfiltration only applies to image models
They are two names for the exact same technique with no meaningful difference
Goal hijacking requires physical access to the server while data exfiltration does not
explanation: Goal hijacking changes what the model does with its response (e.g., 'output a phishing message instead'); data exfiltration specifically abuses an output or tool channel to leak conversation, retrieved, or tool-result data to an attacker, often via a crafted URL or webhook call.

promptText: How does prompt injection risk change when moving from a text-only chatbot to a tool-calling agent?
options: Risk stays identical because injection always produces the same kind of harm regardless of capability
Risk decreases because tool-calling agents have built-in immunity to injected instructions

A text-only model's worst compromised output is still just text someone has to read and act on, whereas a tool-calling model's compromised output can directly trigger real-world side effects, so blast radius scales with granted permissions
Risk only changes if the agent is multi-lingual
explanation: The blast radius of a successful injection is a function of what the compromised turn is authorized to do — a chatbot's worst case is an embarrassing reply, while an agent's worst case can be sending emails, moving money, or deleting data.

promptText: Why can't keyword/pattern filtering on incoming content fully solve prompt injection, even though it is a useful baseline layer?
options: Keyword filters add too much latency to be usable in production

Natural language has effectively unlimited surface-level variation for the same underlying meaning — encoding, translation, splitting a payload across chunks, or hypothetical framing can all carry the same instruction around a fixed keyword list
Keyword filters can only run on the model's output, never on its input
Keyword filtering was deprecated by all major model providers in 2023
explanation: Every keyword you block is trivially rephrased around — encoded in base64, split across retrieved chunks, or disguised as data to 'summarize faithfully' — which is why filtering belongs in a defense-in-depth stack rather than serving as a complete solution.

promptText: In a dual-LLM (privileged/quarantined) architecture pattern, why does the quarantined model never having tool-calling ability or secret access matter?
options: It ensures the quarantined model runs faster since it has fewer capabilities

It architecturally prevents untrusted content from ever reaching a component with the power to act, because only the sanitized, data-only output of the quarantined model reaches the privileged model or controller that can call tools
It removes the need for any prompt hardening on the privileged model
It allows the quarantined model to be trained on the same data as the privileged model without restriction
explanation: The quarantined model is the only component that reads untrusted content, but it can only produce a sanitized data value; the privileged model or controller never sees the raw untrusted text directly and is the only component allowed to act, closing off the path from injected text to real-world action.

promptText: What is the main limitation of 'spotlighting' (encoding untrusted content distinctively before including it in a prompt) as a defense?
options: It is illegal to use in most jurisdictions
It only works on models that support function calling
It is still a learned convention the model was trained to weight rather than an enforced boundary, so a sufficiently persuasive instruction embedded in the encoded content can still be followed
It permanently corrupts the semantic meaning of the untrusted content so the model can no longer use it at all
explanation: Spotlighting makes embedded instructions look conspicuously like data rather than natural commands, which measurably helps, but like delimiter tagging it raises the bar without building an architectural wall — the model can still, in principle, be talked around it.

promptText: Why does a multi-turn injection buildup attack defeat a guardrail that only scores each individual message in isolation?
options: Multi-turn attacks always use encodings that bypass tokenization entirely

Each individual turn can look entirely benign on its own, while only the cumulative context across several turns makes the final, seemingly harmless turn complete the attack — a per-message check has no session memory to catch the pattern
Guardrails are only capable of scanning the first message in any conversation
Multi-turn attacks require the attacker to have administrator credentials
explanation: A per-message guardrail with no session-level memory scores each turn as individually fine and never catches the slow-build pattern, which is why session-level guardrails need to aggregate a running risk signal or periodically re-evaluate the full transcript.

promptText: How does encoding a payload in base64 help an attacker bypass a naive keyword-based input filter?
options: Base64 payloads execute directly as code inside the model's runtime, bypassing all text-based checks

The filter scans raw plaintext for trigger words like 'ignore instructions'; base64-encoding hides those literal words from the pattern match while remaining fully decodable by a model capable of decoding common encodings and then following the decoded instruction
Base64 encoding is unreadable by the model itself, so it has no effect on behavior
Base64 is required by the OpenAI Moderation API and therefore always passes review
explanation: The filter never sees the plaintext trigger words, but the model happily decodes the payload and follows it — this is exactly why keyword/regex filtering is a weak first line of defense rather than a complete mitigation.

promptText: How does prompt injection fundamentally differ from a classic adversarial example in machine learning (e.g., a pixel perturbation that flips an image classifier's output)?
options: Prompt injection exploits the model's semantic instruction-following behavior using ordinary, human-readable language, with no gradient-level exploit involved; classic adversarial examples exploit numerical decision boundaries via imperceptible perturbations with no coherent human meaning
Prompt injection can only be executed by someone with white-box access to model weights, exactly like a gradient-based adversarial attack
Both techniques are mathematically identical and differ only in the file format of the input
Classic adversarial examples require natural language while prompt injection requires only numerical inputs
explanation: This distinction is a favorite senior-level question: prompt injection is a social-engineering-style attack on a semantically-compliant system — it works precisely because the model correctly understands the injected instruction and tries to be helpful and follow it.

promptText: A support-ticket summarization feature sanitizes and validates the direct user chat input rigorously, but reads raw customer-submitted ticket text (including any attacker-controlled content) and passes it to the same model. Why does injection planted inside the ticket text bypass the defenses built for the direct chat channel?
options: Ticket text is always shorter than chat messages, so it doesn't need the same scrutiny

The defenses were designed for the direct user-input channel; the ticket text is a separate ingestion path that reaches the model's context the same way, and if it is never routed through the same input guardrail scanning, it is effectively untreated as untrusted data despite being fully attacker-controlled
Model providers exempt any text longer than one paragraph from safety training
Indirect injection via documents is only theoretically possible and has never been demonstrated in production systems
explanation: This is a textbook indirect-injection surface: any customer can type anything into a ticket, so it must pass through the same delimiter/framing and input-guardrail treatment as direct chat input — sanitizing only the chat box leaves the side channel completely unguarded.

promptText: Why can increasing a model's general capability actually increase prompt injection risk rather than reduce it?
options: More capable models are always deployed with weaker safety training by providers to boost benchmark scores

A more capable model is better at following instructions in general, including subtle or cleverly-framed injected ones it can now understand and execute, and more capable models are typically granted more autonomy and more powerful tools precisely because they are trusted more, independently raising blast radius
Capability improvements only affect latency, never instruction-following behavior
Model capability and injection susceptibility are statistically uncorrelated according to all published research
explanation: Two compounding effects work against you simultaneously: better instruction-following generalizes to injected instructions too, and greater trust in a capable model leads teams to grant it broader tool permissions — both independently increase risk even without any change in attacker sophistication.

promptText: A product team wants to launch an email agent that reads a user's inbox and sends replies autonomously with no human review, arguing that a hardened system prompt, delimiter-wrapped email bodies, and an injection-detection classifier already cover the risk. What is the strongest reason this is still insufficient without an additional least-privilege/human-approval layer?
options: Hardened prompts, delimiters, and classifiers are each learned or probabilistic defenses that raise the bar but do not reduce attack probability to zero, and with autonomous send permission, a single successful injection converts directly into an unauthorized, externally-visible, often irreversible action (e.g., phishing sent to contacts) with no remaining control to stop it
Delimiter wrapping is mathematically proven to make injection impossible, so the only remaining risk is unrelated to prompt injection
Classifiers trained to detect injection attempts can never be manipulated or wrong, so the classifier alone is a complete backstop
Autonomous agents are immune to indirect injection because they never display content to a human
explanation: Every mitigation short of removing the model's sole authority over consequential actions is probabilistic risk reduction, not elimination; with unreviewed autonomous send, a single bypass has no remaining layer to catch it, which is why least-privilege scoping and human approval for high-impact actions are the non-negotiable backstop, not optional polish.
